title: The sound of Persian
hookLine: Rumi's rhyme and rhythm are lost in English
tomorrow: is a Muslim poet okay at a Catholic memorial?

cards: Zoe's question tonight is about a song. Inés's grandmother loved an old Latin hymn, and Inés wants it played at the memorial. Her cousin says nobody understands Latin, so what's the point?

Zoe asks Ray, her friend the retired philosophy teacher, and he laughs: you're asking whether sound can carry what words can't. That's yesterday's question in a new coat. What is Rumi in English missing?

teach.b: Start with a story his followers tell. Rumi was walking through the goldsmiths' market in Konya when he heard the hammers in Salah al-Din Zarkub's shop, beating gold in rhythm.
And he began to turn, right there in the street.

teach.h: DON'T STOP, EVEN IF THE GOLD SPOILS.
teach.b: Salah al-Din saw him and told his workers: don't stop. Keep hammering, even if the gold is spoiled. The goldsmith became one of Rumi's closest companions.
The tradition's word for this is sama, which means listening. In Sufi teaching, sound, music, a recited line, even a hammer's beat, can open the heart toward God before the mind catches up.
It's why Mevlevi gatherings turn to music. And it's why Rumi loses so much in English. His poems are built of meter and rhyme.
In Persian, yesterday's ghazal keeps landing on the same sound at the end of its couplets, reha kon, mobtala kon, like a knock at a door.
English keeps the meaning and drops the knock. So the honest answer to the cousin, in this tradition: hearing comes first.

how: In Sufi gatherings, sama (listening) means hearing poetry and music as devotion; Mevlevis turn to music in their ceremony, and Rumi's ghazals are sung and recited aloud, not only read silently.

games.q: what does “the sound of persian” mean?
o: the drumbeat that opens a Mevlevi ceremony
the rhythm and rhyme of Rumi's poems in Persian
an accent Persian speakers keep for holy texts

games.q: the hammer and the sound: tap the pairs.
p: the goldsmith whose hammers Rumi heard
listening, as a road toward God
the goldsmith's order to his workers
the sound the ghazal keeps landing on

s: an English Rumi carries his rhyme and meter too
English can keep the meaning, but the Persian's meter and rhyme don't come across.
the Sufi practice of hearing poetry and music as a road toward God.
in the story, the goldsmith stopped work so Rumi could think
he told his workers to keep hammering, even if the gold was spoiled.

games.q: at a funeral, a hymn is sung in a language you don't speak. your cousin whispers, 'what's the point if no one understands?' what would Rumi's tradition say?
o: listening comes first; the sound itself can carry what words can't.
there's no point; a hymn only counts if it's understood.
the point is to show how old the family's faith is.
games.why: sama means listening. Rumi began to turn at a goldsmith's hammers; the sound opened the door before the meaning did.

practice: If you can, play a short recording of Persian poetry being recited, and don't try to translate it. If not, listen to one steady sound near you: a fan, the rain, a clock. Let the rhythm do the work for two minutes.

wordCard.voice: The sound of Persian: the meter, rhyme and repeated endings Rumi wrote in, which English can't carry. Sama starts with listening.

orig.note: Arabic and Persian: listening. In Sufism, hearing poetry and music as devotion.

carryVoice: Here's the line: the sound, before the meaning, the way a hammer started Rumi turning. Seven days with Rumi again.
